title: Randomized complexity of online labeling
formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal amortized expected number of relabelings per insertion or deletion for randomized online list labeling with at most \(n\) live items and labels in \([2n]\), against an oblivious adversary. The target is one asymptotic rate \(f(n)\) with a matching upper bound and lower bound in the model below.
why: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.

category_assignment.reason: Maintains ordered labels in a bounded array and charges relocations, a general representation primitive.

importance.reason: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.

sentences: An ordered list is stored using a fixed range of numerical labels.
Insertions and deletions must preserve label order while keeping spare labels available.
The cost counts how many existing items receive a different label.
Randomization achieves nearly logarithmic expected amortized cost in the cited result.
The remaining task is to determine the optimal asymptotic rate for constant slack.

definitions: Fix a capacity \(n\ge2\) and start with an empty ordered list. An insertion specifies the rank at which a new distinct item enters the list; a deletion names a live item. The list never contains more than \(n\) items. After each update the algorithm assigns distinct labels from \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\) to the live items, in strictly increasing list order. Cost is one for the update plus the total number of relabelings of surviving items during it; assigning a label to the new item costs at most one additional unit. The input sequence is fixed independently of all random choices. Only relabelings are charged: local computation, rank search and auxiliary metadata are free, so this is a movement-cost model, not a word-RAM running-time target. An upper rate \(f\ge1\) means a uniform online algorithm and a constant \(C\) satisfy expected total cost at most \(C(n+M f(n))\) for every capacity and every finite valid sequence of \(M\) updates. For tightness, every algorithm and every rate \(g\) permitting such a bound must have \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\). Constants are independent of the sequence and capacity. The array has fixed constant slack; other label-universe regimes are outside this card. The algorithm is a fixed finite computable program taking the capacity as input, without advice or an oracle, and may use independent fair random bits. It receives updates sequentially, has no access to future updates, and must finish each operation almost surely with a valid ordered labeling. Its finite local computation and auxiliary storage are not charged by the movement objective. An oblivious sequence may depend on the algorithm and the capacity but not on the sampled random bits or observed random labels. The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices for that fixed full sequence. A surviving item changed more than once during an update is counted for each relabeling; labels of live items must be valid at the end of the update. Here \(f(n)\) and competing rates \(g(n)\) concern integer capacities \(n\ge2\), and the asymptotic lower comparison is as \(n\to\infty\).

context_blocks.text: List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The original seminar question concerned randomized online labeling broadly. The retained benchmark selects constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary, matching the subsequently specified researcher-linked variant. The answer requires a tight asymptotic rate, rather than just the analysis of one named algorithm.

answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously defined rate \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) and complete Lean-checked upper and matching lower bounds up to constant factors in the stated expected amortized movement model. The upper bound must provide one uniform online algorithm with expected total cost \(O(n+Mf(n))\) for every capacity and oblivious valid sequence. The lower bound must establish the stated \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\) requirement for every competing permitted algorithm and achievable rate. An unbounded polylogarithmic factor or a lower bound only for a restricted algorithm family does not meet the target.
